title: Splitting the Repair Agent's Work
summary: Work through Splitting the Repair Agent's Work.

blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Splitting the Repair Agent's Work**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Multi-Agent Coordination, § Splitting the Repair Agent's Work
blocks.md: The repair agent (a later section) has so far fixed a connection-pool race, a change confined to one module that a single controller holds comfortably in one context. Its next assignment is wider: migrate an authentication module across a repository, a change that reaches every caller of the module's interface and is exactly the kind of repair task that tempts a split. The task naturally splits into two coupled changes: revising an internal interface and updating its downstream callers.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Credit-window flow control matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: A credit window enforces free plus outstanding equal to W, bounding in-flight payload and, by Little's law, mean staleness at W/mu, which per-agent token budgets cannot do.

questions.q: The section **Splitting the Repair Agent's Work** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A credit window enforces free plus outstanding equal to W, bounding in-flight payload and, by Little's law, mean staleness at W/mu, which per-agent token budgets cannot do.
An all-results barrier meets a deadline with probability F(t)^N, and a k-of-N rule recovers most of it only when results are interchangeable.
Dynamic spawning makes the execution graph nondeterministic, so the runtime enforces fan-out, concurrency, depth, and deadline bounds and reserves each child's maximum liability before it starts.

Delegation is justified only if it beats a capable single controller on the same tasks, criteria, evidence access, concurrency, and resource ceilings, scored on end-to-end acceptance with every initiated task counted.
